extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, mathematics-education researchers, and instructors concerned with students' proof skills
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and improving students' ability to construct mathematical proofs (especially in abstract algebra) by identifying the strategic knowledge types that distinguish expert (doctoral) from novice (undergraduate) performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to construct proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to construct proofs is an important skill for all mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper highlights that students may know and be able to apply the facts required to prove a statement yet still fail to produce a proof; thus the criterion emphasizes synthesizing known facts and procedures into a coherent proof rather than mere factual knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of syntactic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the syntactic knowledge that they had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undergraduates often fail to construct proofs because they cannot use the syntactic (manipulative/structural) knowledge they possess; ability to translate facts into syntactic manipulations and reasoning is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing which facts and theorems to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of how to choose which facts and theorems to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as one of the central types of 'strategic knowledge'—effective proof construction requires selecting relevant results from among many available facts/theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of powerful proof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the powerful proof techniques in abstract algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctoral students appeared to possess awareness of powerful, domain-specific proof techniques; assessing whether a student knows and can deploy these techniques is a dimension of strategic competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of which theorems are most important
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing which theorems are most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts know which results are central or frequently useful; part of strategic knowledge is prioritizing certain theorems when constructing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement about when particular facts/theorems are useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing when particular facts and theorems are likely to be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond knowing individual results, students must judge applicability contexts—recognizing problem features that make a theorem relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding when to use symbol manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing when one should or should not try and prove theorems using symbol manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic choice between attempting direct symbol manipulation/computation versus pursuing more conceptual or structural proof approaches; experts reportedly make this decision effectively.
